## Facebook Use Predicts Declines in Subjective Well-Being in Young Adults

Ethan Kross 1 * , Philippe Verduyn 2 , Emre Demiralp 1 , Jiyoung Park 1 , David Seungjae Lee 1 , Natalie Lin 1 , Holly Shablack 1 , John Jonides 1 , Oscar Ybarra 1

1 Psychology Department, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, United States of America, 2 Psychology Department, University of Leuven, Leuven, Belgium

## Abstract

Over 500 million people interact daily with Facebook. Yet, whether Facebook use influences subjective well-being over time is unknown. We addressed this issue using experience-sampling, the most reliable method for measuring in-vivo behavior and psychological experience. We text-messaged people five times per day for two-weeks to examine how Facebook use influences the two components of subjective well-being: how people feel moment-to-moment and how satisfied they are with their lives. Our results indicate that Facebook use predicts negative shifts on both of these variables over time. The more people used Facebook at one time point, the worse they felt the next time we text-messaged them; the more they used Facebook over two-weeks, the more their life satisfaction levels declined over time. Interacting with other people ''directly'' did not predict these negative outcomes. They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression. On the surface, Facebook provides an invaluable resource for fulfilling the basic human need for social connection. Rather than enhancing well-being, however, these findings suggest that Facebook may undermine it.

hypotheses.statement: Facebook use during the interval between two text messages predicts a decline in momentary affective well-being at the later time point, controlling for earlier affect.

hypotheses.statement: Average Facebook use over the 14-day period predicts a decline in life satisfaction (cognitive well-being) from pre to post, controlling for baseline life satisfaction and average emotion.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: we analyzed whether people's average Facebook use over the 14-day period predicted their life satisfaction at the end of the study, controlling for baseline life satisfaction and average emotion levels over the 14-day period

hypotheses.statement: Direct (face-to-face or phone) social interaction does not produce the same declines in affective and cognitive well-being that Facebook use does.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: An alternative explanation for these results is that any form of social interaction undermines wellbeing. Because we also asked people to indicate how frequently they interacted with other people ''directly'' since the last time we text messaged them, we were able to test this idea.

hypotheses.statement: The Facebook-use effect on well-being is not moderated by number of Facebook friends, perceived network support, depressive symptoms, loneliness, gender, self-esteem, time of participation, or motivation for using Facebook.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: They were also not moderated by the size of people's Facebook networks, their perceived supportiveness, motivation for using Facebook, gender, loneliness, self-esteem, or depression.

hypotheses.statement: Facebook use and direct social contact interact to predict changes in affective and cognitive well-being.

findings.notes: FAMILY DEFINITION IS DOING A LOT OF WORK HERE AND THE CAVEAT MUST TRAVEL WITH THE NUMBER. The family I supplied is broad -- every significance test in the Results -- and under it, both results that are significant at exact p (.02 and .02, the two life-satisfaction models) fall below every correction threshold. But those two are not independent claims: they are the SAME cognitive well-being outcome fitted with and without a loneliness covariate, so counting them as two is itself generous. Under the narrower and quite defensible family of two primary outcomes (affective, cognitive), Bonferroni alpha is .025 and the cognitive result at p=.02 survives. The affective result is untouched under any reading: at chi-square 28.90 its true p is around 8e-08, orders of magnitude below any threshold. So the honest statement is that the paper's FIRST headline claim is robust to multiplicity and its SECOND is fragile to it, and the paper applies and mentions no correction anywhere. A further, unquantifiable factor: at least twelve moderation tests and two interaction tests are reported only as 'ps > .16' and 'ps > .44', so the true comparison count exceeds the 15 counted here and this is a FLOOR on the multiplicity problem.

consequence.explanation: Under the broad family, the abstract's second claim -- that the more people used Facebook over two weeks, the more their life satisfaction declined (t(73) = -2.39, p = .02) -- does not survive Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg or Benjamini-Yekutieli correction; under a two-outcome family it does.

computed.method: A reading of what the paper does and does not print. The participant-level analytic n is never stated; the only trace of it is the residual df chain, which steps down by exactly one as each additional covariate is added (73 with 3 predictors, 72 with 4, 71 with 5) -- an internally coherent pattern. No sample size was computed from it here.

findings.reproduction: no command applies -- this records a value the paper never prints, not an arithmetic result
findings.notes: The paper reports the observation count (4,589) but never the participant count entering the OLS life-satisfaction models; a reader must infer it from the degrees of freedom. The df chain is at least self-consistent, stepping down by one per added covariate exactly as it should, which is a point in the paper's favour -- and I used that chain as my working n elsewhere in this sweep, labelling it an inference every time. Recorded as indeterminate because the figure is genuinely absent rather than wrong. It matters because Table 1's correlations, the twelve moderation tests and all three OLS models depend on an n the reader is never told.

findings.notes: No a-priori power analysis and no sample-size justification appear anywhere. This is unremarkable for a 2013 experience-sampling paper and is NOT offered as a criticism of the authors' conduct; it is recorded because it bears directly on the moderation nulls above. The participant-level tests run on roughly 77 people and the paper itself describes its effects as 'small', so the twelve null moderation tests are where an unstated power assumption does the most work.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Facebook use predicts declines in affect and life satisfaction over time. Interacting with Facebook during one time period (Time1-2) leads people to feel worse later on during the same day (T2) controlling for how they felt initially (T1); values are regression weights from multilevel analyses (Panel A). Average Facebook use over the course of the 14-day experience-sampling period predicts decreases in life satisfaction over time; values are standardized regression weights from OLS regression analysis (Panel B). * p , .05, ** p , .01, *** p , .001.

panels.shows: Path diagram of the lagged multilevel model: T1-2 Facebook use predicting T2 affect while controlling for T1 affect, annotated with regression weights and significance stars.
Path diagram of the OLS model: mean Facebook use over the 14 days predicting post life satisfaction controlling for pre life satisfaction, annotated with standardized regression weights.

unchecked.reason: Both panels are path diagrams annotated with regression weights. The two weights named in the caption's prose (the multilevel B and the standardized OLS beta) also appear in the Results text and were verified there, but the diagrams very likely also print the AUTOREGRESSIVE paths (T1 affect to T2 affect; pre to post life satisfaction) and possibly their significance stars, and those coefficients appear nowhere in the text or in Table 1. I did not run figure extraction, so any value carried only by the figure is unchecked. This is a specific, locatable gap in this review rather than a generic caveat.

The table states NO sample size, for either the within-person or the between-person half, and no n for it appears anywhere in the paper. Significance is shown only as asterisk thresholds, with no exact p-values. Only the single borderline cell (r = .22*) was close enough to .05 to be testable at all, and it was tested at the df-implied n of 77 with a consistent result. Every other cell is either far from a threshold or would require an n the paper does not supply.

unchecked.location: Statcheck was deliberately NOT run over the body text
unchecked.reason: This PDF's font encoding renders every minus sign as the digit 2 and every chi-square as 'x2', so 't(73) = -2.39' appears in the text layer as 't (73) = 2 2.39'. Feeding that to statcheck would have it parse mangled statistics and report inconsistencies that are artifacts of extraction rather than properties of the paper. Instead I read each of the 17 test statistics against both the docling body text and the per-page text, and verified every one individually with recalc_stat_to_p. Coverage of the NHST statistics is therefore complete; only the automated scanner was skipped, and deliberately.

Not applicable and deliberately not run. The paper contains exactly one table and it is a correlation matrix, not a table of means and SDs. There is no second block of summary statistics to compare it against, within the paper or across studies.

Deliberately not run. The paper's effects are small (standardized beta = -.124 for the life-satisfaction outcome), which is entirely typical for social-psychological field data, and the authors themselves flag the effects as 'small' in their Caveats section. There is no implausibly LARGE effect for this check to adjudicate.

unchecked.location: GRIM on the SWLS, Social Provision Scale and UCLA Loneliness means
unchecked.reason: All three are means of multi-item composites, so their granularity is 1/(k*n) rather than 1/n. At roughly 80 participants and 5 or more items the attainable steps are finer than the second decimal place, so GRIM has no discriminating power and would return 'consistent' for essentially any printed value. Running it would manufacture false reassurance rather than evidence.
